title: Building Generative Image & Video models at Scale - Sander Dieleman, Google DeepMind

primary.label: Model Foundations & Behavior

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary object is the diffusion model itself—its architecture, training dynamics, sampling behavior, spectral auto-regression properties, and scaling considerations. The focus is on generative image and video models for creative content production, with general-purpose model foundation insights applicable across modalities. Covers pretraining (data curation, representation, architecture, training at scale), post-training (control signals, preference tuning), and inference (sampling, guidance, distillation). Requires deep familiarity with diffusion models, Fourier analysis, latent representations, and distributed training. A structured conference presentation with slides, visualizations, and an extended Q&A session. All twelve evidence anchors are graded 'said_in_transcript' with direct excerpts from the talk.

summary:
Sander Dieleman, a Google DeepMind research scientist on the generative media team (VEO, NanoBanana), presents a behind-the-scenes talk on training diffusion-based image and video models at scale. He outlines eight topics: data curation, representation, modeling (diffusion mechanisms), network architecture, training at scale, sampling and guidance, distillation, and control signals. Diffusion models are the dominant paradigm for audio-visual generation, contrasting with language modeling's reliance on autoregression.

Data curation is critically important and underrated. Time spent improving data can be a better investment than tweaking models, though specific practices remain proprietary.

For representation, direct pixel-space training is infeasible at scale. Learned autoencoders compress inputs into latent representations preserving spatial topology and semantic content while reducing resolution and adding channels. Standard codecs are avoided because they obscure structure needed for generative modeling.

For modeling, Dieleman explains diffusion: corruption adds Gaussian noise destroying fine detail first, a denoiser learns to reverse this, and sampling takes small iterative steps with optional noise re-injection. Fourier analysis shows diffusion is spectral auto-regression—generating coarse-to-fine.

For network architecture, U-Nets were the initial choice; transformers also work with fully bidirectional attention. For video, there is a tension between autoregression and diffusion: most modern models jointly noise the entire 3D volume; a hybrid approach does autoregression in time with diffusion per frame (e.g., Genie).

Training at scale requires parallelism and sharding. JAX provides tooling for automatic sharding, designed with TPUs in mind. Models are still smaller than LLMs, partly because guidance lets them punch above their weight.

Sampling involves stochastic vs. deterministic tradeoffs. Guidance trades diversity for quality by amplifying the delta between conditioned and unconditioned predictions, requiring two evaluations per step. It is universally used.

Distillation reduces sampling steps. Consistency models predict the endpoint instead of the tangent, though multi-step intervals are often needed.

Control signals go beyond text prompts to include reference-based generation (e.g., putting yourself in a video via photo conditioning), camera motion control, and event timing. These are often introduced in post-training since pre-training data lacks them. Preference tuning (RL/DPO) also occurs in post-training.

The Q&A reveals: guidance contributes to model style but post-training plays a bigger role; high guidance causes oversaturation; varying guidance scale across sampling helps; guidance works best with a semantic gap between conditioning signal and target; more sampling steps improve quality up to a point (piecewise linear approximation of non-linear path; rectified flow research addresses this); conditioning can be inserted via extra tokens or broadcasting; deterministic sampling (no noise re-injection) is required for consistency model distillation.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Sander Dieleman introduces himself as a Google DeepMind research scientist on the generative media team (VEO, NanoBanana). He outlines eight topics: data curation, representation, modeling, network architecture, training at scale, sampling and guidance, distillation, and control signals. He notes diffusion is the dominant paradigm for audio-visual generation, contrasting with autoregression in language modeling.

sections.title: Data Curation
sections.summary: Dieleman emphasizes data curation is critically important and underrated. Academic research uses predefined datasets for comparability, but production requires careful data inspection. Time improving data can beat tweaking models, though specifics are proprietary.

sections.title: Representation
sections.summary: Direct pixel-space training is infeasible at scale. Learned autoencoders compress inputs into latent representations preserving spatial topology and grid structure while reducing resolution and adding channels. Standard codecs are avoided because they obscure structure. Latents preserve semantic content and compress local texture. Video tensors can shrink by up to two orders of magnitude.

sections.title: Modeling: Diffusion Mechanism
sections.summary: Dieleman explains diffusion in detail: corruption adds Gaussian noise destroying fine detail first, a denoiser learns to reverse this, and sampling takes small iterative steps. One-step denoising is ill-posed, producing blurry averages. Noise re-injection prevents error accumulation. Fourier analysis shows image spectra follow power laws while noise is flat, making diffusion spectral auto-regression—generating coarse-to-fine.

sections.title: Network Architecture
sections.summary: U-Nets, originally designed for image segmentation, were the initial architecture for denoisers, used in Stable Diffusion. Transformers also work, using fully bidirectional attention (no causal mask), making them slightly more expressive than LLM transformers. For video, there is a tension between autoregression and diffusion: fully autoregressive models flatten the 3D cube into a sequence, most modern models jointly noise the entire 3D volume, and a hybrid approach does autoregression in time with diffusion per frame (e.g., Genie, useful for real-time generation).

sections.title: Training at Scale
sections.summary: Models are scaled up with more parameters, though still smaller than LLMs—partly because guidance lets them punch above their weight. Data parallelism suffices up to a point, then model parallelism is needed. JAX provides tooling for automatic sharding and communication minimization between chips.

sections.title: Sampling & Guidance
sections.summary: Stochastic sampling (with noise re-injection) is more robust to error accumulation; deterministic sampling provides one-to-one mapping between initial noise and samples. Guidance trades diversity for quality by making two predictions (with and without conditioning), computing the delta, and amplifying it. This requires two model evaluations per step but massively improves quality. Guidance is now universally used. GLIDE paper examples demonstrate quality improvement and diversity reduction.

sections.title: Distillation
sections.summary: Distillation in diffusion reduces the number of sampling steps, not model size. The sampling trajectory is a non-linear path through input space; the model predicts tangents. Consistency models instead predict where the path ends up, enabling one-step sampling. In practice, one-step sampling usually doesn't work well, so multi-step intervals are used.

sections.title: Control Signals
sections.summary: Models are only as useful as our ability to influence their outputs. Text prompts are the canonical conditioning method but increasingly people want reference-based generation (e.g., putting yourself in a video by conditioning on a photo), explicit camera motion control, and event timing control. These conditioning signals are often unavailable in pre-training data, so they are introduced in post-training. Preference tuning via reinforcement learning or direct preference optimization also occurs in post-training.

sections.title: Q&A
sections.summary: Dieleman answers audience questions. On model style: post-training makes models opinionated by selecting a sliver of the pre-training distribution; high guidance causes oversaturation; varying guidance scale across the sampling procedure (ramping up in the middle) gives better trade-offs. On text diffusion guidance: the same procedure applies, but guidance works best with a semantic gap between conditioning signal and generation target—it works well for text prompts but poorly for low-level signals like segmentation masks. On JAX vs. PyTorch: JAX was designed from the start for TPUs and multi-chip scaling, though PyTorch can also do model parallelism. On more sampling steps: quality improves up to a point because finite steps approximate a non-linear path as piecewise linear; rectified flow/re-flow research aims to produce straighter paths. On camera control signals: the right semantically abstract representation must be found; conditioning can be inserted via extra tokens or broadcasting to all tokens. On deterministic sampling: omitting noise re-injection yields a fully deterministic model, useful for bidirectional data-noise mapping and required as a teacher for consistency model distillation.
